binders: Real-valued random variables X1,...,XN on a common probability space.
A real threshold t with t>=0.
A positive absolute constant c, uniform over N, the probability space, the family, and t.
hypotheses: The random variables X1,...,XN are mutually independent.
conclusions: For every t>=0, P{|sum_{i=1}^N X_i|>=t} <= 2 exp[-c min(t^2/(sum_{i=1}^N ||X_i||_psi1^2), t/(max_{1<=i<=N} ||X_i||_psi1))].
definitions_and_conventions: The summed random variable is S=sum_{i=1}^N X_i.
The event is two-sided because it uses |S|>=t.
The minimum selects the quadratic regime t^2/V or the linear regime t/K.
The symbol ||X_i||_psi1 denotes the established sub-exponential norm from the preceding section.
implicit_context: N is nonzero because the source lists X1,...,XN and takes a maximum over their indices.
All variables are the same probability space; otherwise their sum and mutual independence would not have the displayed meaning.
The word absolute means that c does not depend on N, the variables, their distribution, or t.
The psi-one norms are nonnegative, so V and K are nonnegative and K>0 is equivalent to at least one component having positive psi-one norm.
When K>0, V>0 as well, and both displayed quotients have their ordinary real meanings.

details: There is a universal positive constant c for the theorem.
After a qualifying finite family is fixed, the inequality holds for every real t>=0.
The random quantity is the unweighted sum of all X_i.
The absolute value makes the conclusion a two-sided tail estimate.
Its denominator is exactly the sum of the squared individual psi-one norms.
Its denominator is exactly the maximum individual psi-one norm.
The printed real quotients are unambiguously defined when K>0.
The theorem does not state how to interpret either quotient when every psi-one norm is zero.

undebatable_constraints: The family is finite and nonempty in the source's X1,...,XN indexing convention.
The variables are independent, mean zero, and sub-exponential.
The threshold range is every t>=0.
The tail event is |sum_i X_i|>=t, not merely sum_i X_i>=t.
The exponent is -c times the minimum of two terms.
The first term is exactly t^2 divided by sum_i ||X_i||_psi1^2.
The second term is exactly t divided by max_i ||X_i||_psi1.
The constant c is strictly positive and absolute.
No positivity assumption on max_i ||X_i||_psi1 or sum_i ||X_i||_psi1^2 is printed.
No separate all-zero or zero-scale conclusion is printed.

ambiguities.issue: Both denominators vanish when every psi-one norm is zero.
ambiguities.evidence: The theorem permits mean-zero sub-exponential variables with zero psi-one norm, but its displayed terms are t^2/(sum_i ||X_i||_psi1^2) and t/(max_i ||X_i||_psi1), with no positive-scale hypothesis.
ambiguities.impact: In ordinary real arithmetic the printed formula is undefined for an all-zero-scale family. A formalization must not silently choose between restricting the effective domain to K>0, using extended-real infinite quotients, adopting totalized real division, or adding a separate degenerate branch.

ambiguities.issue: The value at t=0 is especially sensitive to a zero-denominator convention.
ambiguities.evidence: For an all-zero-scale family and t=0, both displayed ratios have the form 0/0, while the source explicitly includes t=0.
ambiguities.impact: Extended-infinity, limiting, and totalized-real interpretations need not assign the same intermediate values, even though some resulting inequalities may still be true. The source supplies no convention.

ambiguities.issue: The exact numerical value of the absolute constant c is unspecified.

ambiguities.impact: A faithful formal statement may existentially quantify a uniform positive constant or instantiate one proved elsewhere, but the source does not justify a particular numerical value.

contract_plain_english: There is a positive universal constant c such that every finite nonempty family of independent, mean-zero, sub-exponential real random variables satisfies a two-sided Bernstein bound: for every t>=0, the probability that the absolute value of their sum is at least t is at most 2 times the exponential of -c multiplied by the smaller of t^2 divided by the sum of squared psi-one norms and t divided by the largest psi-one norm. The printed formula has an unresolved effective-domain defect when all component norms are zero, because both denominators then vanish and the source provides neither a positive-maximum assumption nor a separate degenerate interpretation.
